_comment: Ratio ceilings for tests/bench/gate.py. Each key is <case>/<suite>/<plaintext bytes>; each
value is the most that case may cost relative to a straight-line implementation of the same
algorithm with the same cipher, measured in the same process (tests/bench/bench_support.h
explains the references).
Every ceiling is 1.10, and that one number is the whole claim: this project's structure — the
envelope bytes, the error mapping, the buffer handling, the OPENSSL_cleanse calls — must cost
under 10% on top of the cryptography it performs. It is not a performance target so much as an
assertion that there is no hidden per-call work: a fetch that stopped being cached, a buffer
reallocated per row, one more copy of the plaintext would each land far outside it.
Three runs on ubuntu-24.04 measured every one of the twelve AES-256 ratios between 0.986 and
1.029, with a run-to-run spread of 1.025x. So 1.10 clears the worst observation by 7% and the
observed variance by roughly double. The AES-192 and AES-128 rows take the same ceiling
because the claim is the same — the suites share every line of code except the fetched
cipher — and each divides by a reference running its own cipher, so the round count cancels.
The measurements, per suite, are in docs/perf.md.
open_session and seal_det_session are the per-UDF_INIT paths of design A11 -- a scheduled
context kept across rows, and a derived nonce_key kept across rows. Each divides by a reference
that keeps the same state, so the ratio is still structure over algorithm with the setup already
paid; what the reuse *saves* is the un-gated open_session_vs_open and seal_det_session_vs_seal_det.
Their ceilings are wider at the small sizes, and that is arithmetic rather than tolerance: the
structure around one open -- the envelope parse, the suite lookups, the constant-time compare of
the 32-byte key copy -- costs the same ~20 ns whether the algorithm under it costs 300 ns (a fresh
context) or 120 ns (a kept one). 10% of 120 ns is less than the key compare alone. 1.35 at 16 and
256 bytes, 1.15 at 4 KiB and 1.10 at 64 KiB are provisional, set from one container run on a busy
laptop (open_session 1.04-1.40, seal_det_session 0.92-1.21), and are to be replaced from three CI
runs before this is relied on -- docs/perf.md records both.
That this is gateable at all is a property of the references. An earlier version divided all
three encrypt cases by a bare seal, which spread seal_det by 2.69x across identical runners —
an HMAC-dominated measurement over an AES-only reference is the runner's SHA-to-AES throughput
ratio, not a property of this code.
A case that exists with no ceiling here is a violation, not a pass: adding a benchmark must
force a decision about what it is allowed to cost.
Raising a ceiling needs a PR that says on what hardware, against which server version, and why
the regression is acceptable, and updates docs/perf.md in the same change.
